title: Palantir Looks Cheap Among AI Software Stocks, UBS Says — Why PLTR Could Have More Room To Run
detail:
Palantir Looks Cheap Among AI Software Stocks, UBS Says — Why PLTR Could Have More Room To Run
Palantir Looks Cheap Among AI Software Stocks, UBS Says — Why PLTR Could Have More Room To Run · Stocktwits
Aveek Bhowmik
Tue, September 15, 2026 at 11:39 AM MST 2 min read
PLTR
Trade PLTR on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

UBS raised its price target for Palantir, while maintaining a 'Buy' rating.

The brokerage believes Palantir deserves a premium for its exposure to AI, data, and modern defense technology.

20 of 31 analysts tracked by Koyfin rate PLTR 'Buy' or 'Strong Buy.'

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) looks relatively cheap compared with AI-linked software peers, according to UBS, which expects the stock to rebound as demand for its artificial intelligence-linked software services gains traction.

At the time of writing on Tuesday afternoon, PLTR stock was trading nearly 1.7% higher.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

UBS Raises PLTR Price Target

UBS reiterated a 'Buy' rating on Palantir and raised its price target to $250 from $220, implying 44% upside from Monday's close.

"Last week we attended Palantir's AIPCon customer/leadership event … our view of Palantir as the best AI enabler in the market (making frontier models/AI useful in large enterprises) was if anything bolstered by these conversations [with Palantir executives and customers], and demand momentum seems robust," the UBS analyst wrote in a report on Tuesday, according to a report in CNBC.

Palantir provides AI-integrated software platforms to clients including the Department of Defense, enabling users to analyze massive data sets.

Valuation Looks Attractive

PLTR stock now trades at 51 times expected free cash flow for 2027, despite Palantir having "the highest growth and margin profiles across software," according to UBS.

At current prices, the stock is particularly attractive versus peers such as Snowflake and CrowdStrike, UBS wrote, as reported by CNBC.

The brokerage said the "valuation discount derives largely from investor concerns about a near-term growth rate peak and the potential that the model providers begin to target the data software layer."

"Palantir deserves a material multiple premium given its leading position in three key growth areas – AI, data and modern defense tech, making it a relatively cheap stock," the brokerage wrote.

PLTR Stock: Stocktwits Retail Sentiment

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for PLTR was 'bearish,' unchanged in the past 24 hours, while message volume remained 'normal' during the same period.

The UBS call matches the consensus on Wall Street. According to data from Koyfin, 20 of the 31 analysts covering PLTR rate it 'Buy' and 'Strong Buy,' while nine rate it 'Hold' and one each rate it 'Sell' and 'Strong Sell.'

Shares of Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) and Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) are up 40% and 38%, respectively, since August. Both rank among the 10 most widely held stocks on Robinhood, but the Wall Street analysts below anticipate significant losses for shareholders.

Brent Thill at Jefferies has a sell rating on Palantir. His target price of $80 per share implies 53% downside from the current share price of $172.

Nicolas Owens at Morningstar has a sell rating on SpaceX. His target price of $62 per share implies 58% downside from the current share price of $150.

Here's what investors should know about these popular artificial intelligence stocks.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Palantir Technologies: 53% downside implied by Jefferies' target price

Palantir develops data integration and analytics platforms (Foundry and Gotham) that help customers across the public and private sectors make sense of complex information. The company also designs an adjacent artificial intelligence platform (AIP) that serves as an agnostic large language model (LLM) orchestration tool.

To elaborate, AIP is an application layer that links AI models to company data, systems, and workflows. Its agnostic architecture means customers can select the model best suited to their needs and switch between models as those needs evolve. In addition, AIP lets clients enforce strict governance controls, ensuring AI model providers cannot access sensitive data.

Palantir's financial results have been nothing short of exceptional for the last three years as its software has emerged as the standard in enterprise AI. The company's fundamentals were once again strong in the second quarter. Revenue increased 93% to $1.9 billion, the 12th straight acceleration, and non-GAAP earnings increased 156% to $0.41 per diluted share. Palantir also reported a mind-blowing Rule of 40 score of 155%.

Despite exceptional fundamentals, Brent Thill at Jefferies is concerned the company is not investing enough in its business. Palantir claims it has no real competition, but Anthropic is growing much faster. Anthropic's annual revenue run rate climbed from $1 billion in January 2025 to $65 billion in July 2026. Palantir's annual revenue run rate increased from $3 billion to $7 billion over the same period.

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Palantir Technologies Inc. (PLTR, Financials), the software company known for handling sensitive government and enterprise data, is reportedly putting tougher limits on how some advanced AI models can be used.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 4 Warning Signs with PLTR.

Is PLTR fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

PLTR GF Value chart

Palantir, Nvidia and Booz Allen Hamilton could restrict or stop using models from Anthropic and OpenAI unless the companies provide stronger guarantees around customer data and intellectual property, Reuters reported, citing The Information.

Palantir has pushed Anthropic for irrevocable zero-data-retention guarantees before making its models available through Palantir software.

Nvidia is taking a different approach. The chipmaker reportedly limits Anthropic models to less sensitive work and uses its own Nemotron models for some internal tasks.

Booz Allen has also barred employees from using Anthropic's commercial model for proprietary cybersecurity work. The concerns come as AI labs face more scrutiny over how usage logs and customer information are stored.

Microsoft may have an opening. The company is reportedly pitching isolated cloud environments and its own AI products to customers worried about data exposure.

For investors, this adds a new layer to the AI race. The winners may not simply have the strongest models. They may also be the companies customers trust with their most sensitive information.

title: Oklo Has Massive Potential Due to Artificial Intelligence, but the Stock Is Sinking. Here's What I'd Do

Oklo Has Massive Potential Due to Artificial Intelligence, but the Stock Is Sinking. Here's What I'd Do
David Jagielski, CPA, The Motley Fool

NVDA

Trading disclosure

One of the ways investors have taken advantage of opportunities related to artificial intelligence (AI) is to invest in energy companies that can also benefit from the boom related to next-gen technologies. Rather than investing in Nvidia or Palantir Technologies and more obvious AI stocks, many investors have turned to much smaller companies, with potentially much more upside in the long run.

Oklo (NYSE:OKLO) is a great example of that. It's not making chips or AI-related products and services, but it can potentially play a big role in the build-out of data centers, by providing them with the ongoing energy needs they're going to require via its powerhouses.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Last year, it soared 238% in value. Thus far in 2026, however, it's been a far different story, with the energy stock losing roughly half of its value. What's gone wrong with Oklo, and is it worth buying right now? Here's what I do with it.

Image source: Getty Images.

Why Oklo might be too risky to buy today

Oklo's stock is down big this year, as the hype has clearly been wearing off the energy stock. While its potential remains promising, the risk is still high as well. It could take years before Oklo generates any meaningful revenue and even longer before it posts a profit. And that's by no means a guarantee, either.

If Oklo's powerhouses prove to be the solutions to the clean energy needs of AI data centers, then the stock may undoubtedly soar in value. However, it's uncertain if things will play out that way. A lot hinges on not only the ongoing need and demand for data centers, but also on Oklo's execution.

Meanwhile, as the company scales and expands its operations, its losses may only intensify. Over the past 12 months, it has incurred $153 million in losses -- that's more than double the $74 million loss it incurred in 2024.

I'd put Oklo's stock on a watch list and forget about it

Although Oklo's stock has a lot of upside related to AI, it also carries tremendous risk. Investors don't need to buy the stock at these early stages to generate a great return from it. Instead, putting it on a watch list and tracking its progress can be a safer route to take.

Then, by waiting to invest in the company when its operations come in full swing and the financial results look encouraging, investors can decide to invest at that stage, when the risk is lower. While the stock would likely be at a far higher price than it is today, given the opportunities in AI, it wouldn't be too late to invest in Oklo and still earn a great return.

title: Does PLTR's One-Year Consolidation Offer a Buying Opportunity?
detail:
Does PLTR's One-Year Consolidation Offer a Buying Opportunity?
Shuvra Shankar Dey
Mon, September 14, 2026 at 10:40 AM MST 5 min read
PLTR
AI
SNOW
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Palantir Technologies' PLTR negligible share-price decline over the past year appears more like a period of consolidation than a deterioration in its investment case. The company continues to benefit from robust demand for its artificial intelligence platforms, expanding commercial adoption and strong government relationships. Its solid growth trajectory and improving operating leverage further support long-term optimism. Against this backdrop, this article examines whether Palantir's recent price stability, underlying business momentum and AI-driven growth prospects present a buying opportunity for investors.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Commercial AI Momentum Should Sustain PLTR's Growth

Palantir's commercial business is emerging as its powerful future growth driver as enterprises accelerate artificial intelligence adoption. Commercial revenues are approaching half of total sales, supported by customers moving beyond pilot programs toward mission-critical deployments. The company's Artificial Intelligence Platform is helping organizations connect models with proprietary data, workflows and operational decisions, strengthening its value across business functions. Larger contract sizes indicate deeper engagement and rising spending among existing clients. That suggests Palantir is building durable relationships rather than relying on customer acquisition. With U.S. operations generating more than four-fifths of revenues, exceptionally strong domestic demand should continue supporting scale, recurring expansion and a widening competitive position in enterprise AI software.

Exceptional Profitability Strengthens PLTR's Bullish Case

Palantir's exceptional margins and cash generation strengthen the bullish case by showing that rapid growth is translating into high-quality earnings. An adjusted gross margin in the mid-80% range in the second quarter of 2026 underscores the scalability of its software model, while an adjusted operating margin above 60% demonstrates significant operating leverage. Free cash flow also exceeded $1.2 billion in the quarter, highlighting the company's ability to convert rising demand into substantial liquidity. Its $9.2 billion cash and short-term Treasury position provides flexibility to invest in product development, expand delivery capacity and pursue strategic opportunities without pressuring the balance sheet. Although cloud-hosting responsibilities created modest gross-margin pressure, faster implementation and deeper customer relationships could outweigh that near-term effect. Overall, PLTR's profitability profile supports sustained, self-funded expansion.

title: Can Palantir Deploy Fast Enough To Move Its Stock Higher?
detail:
Can Palantir Deploy Fast Enough To Move Its Stock Higher?
Trefis Team

GOOG

Photo by ArtsyBee on Pixabay

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock has gained about 28% over the past three months, against under 4% for the S&P 500, and it still trades roughly 19% below its 52-week high. Over the past twelve months it has returned almost nothing. What could move it from here is work Palantir has already sold and has not yet delivered.

What Has Palantir Sold That It Has Not Delivered?

Palantir signed U.S. commercial contracts worth $2.132 billion across their full terms in the June quarter. One multinational technology company that started with a single operating unit has converted to a three-year deal worth nearly $370 million. Palantir's revenue over the trailing twelve months is $6.16 billion. Total remaining deal value across the company ended the June quarter at $13.1 billion, up from $11.8 billion at the end of March, and remaining performance obligations were $4.9 billion at the end of June. Demand is not the missing piece.

Can Palantir Staff Everything It Has Sold?

By its own account, the limiting factor in turning AI into value is the rate of AIP deployment, and AIP is the platform where customers build and run their own AI agents. That deployment work falls to Palantir's forward deployed engineers, or FDEs. In one head-to-head test at a large technology company, Palantir says, an AI lab's deployment team picked a ticketing automation problem and delivered nothing of value, while Palantir's engineers built agent swarms that recommend pricing and packaging changes for the customer's own customers. That work became a contract worth $10 million a year.

That is why the Fujitsu agreement in September matters. Fujitsu renewed its partnership, signing for Palantir AIP and Palantir Foundry, and will serve as a Global FDE Partner. Putting a partner's engineers into deployment widens the channel that turns a signed contract into revenue.

What Would Show You That Rivals Cannot Copy This?

The honest doubt is durability. Selling sovereign AI, which Palantir says is what enterprises now demand, is a pitch any large software vendor can adopt, and nothing in the June quarter settles whether the advantage is technical or simply early. What customers do with the platform is better evidence. Net dollar retention rose to 157%, from 150% in the March quarter, so the buyers already inside are enlarging what they run.

Whether that durability holds matters soon, because this stock does not re-rate slowly. It has gained more than 30% inside two months on seven occasions since 2020, and six of those runs topped 50%. The cleanest test ahead is the U.S. commercial guide, raised in August to at least $3.424 billion for full year 2026, from at least $3.224 billion three months earlier. If deployment capacity binds, it shows up there first. You can see who else is clearing that bar on our screen of companies with rising guidance.
